1:
The title puzzles everyone, the sea in it more than the desert. John Gill denies that Babylon was desert land, and offers instead that a desert lay between it and the countries its destroyers came from, or that the word may be rendered plain, as Chaldea was. Matthew Henry takes the same flat country and adds the water: it was full of lakes, like little seas, and watered by the many streams of the Euphrates; though some, he notes, think it called a desert because a populous city was in time to become one. John Wesley gives both halves briefly, the plain of Babylon and the title of sea earned by the plenty of its waters. Charles Ellicott lists three explanations of the sea: the Euphrates itself, the surging flood of a mingled population, and the description of the whole Euphrates plain, intersected with marshes and lakes, as looking like a sea, which he thinks best. The desert he takes for the catch-word of the following line.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that the heading comes from the prophecy at all. The phrase could hardly have been drawn from it, since the word for sea is never used of the south but always of the west, and there is nothing about a sea in what follows. That makes the heading peculiar rather than late; and against the critics who assign the whole oracle to a prophet at the close of the captivity, and the assertion that no proof is needed that Isaiah was not its author, he sets the possibility that a prophet's insight might stretch over hundreds of years.

Adam Clarke reads the chapter as a composition before reading it as prediction, dividing it into the taking of Babylon at a festival, a short application to the Jews, an obscure word on Dumah, and a word on Arabia. He calls the first section singular for brevity and force, for the rapidity of its movements, and for the energy of colouring with which the action is painted: the prophet sees the storm gathering at a distance, orders go out to the Persians and Medes, and he then enters the action and speaks in the person of Babylon to express the horror that seizes her at the surprise of the city in the season dedicated to festivity.

On the second verse the question is whether the treacherous dealer acts or suffers. Clarke reports that the manuscripts vary in a single letter across the four words, ten omitting it in one place and eight in another, which justifies the Greek version that rendered the clause passively, the plunderer plundered and the destroyer destroyed; he adds the Chaldee and Syriac renderings of the verb by words meaning to spoil and oppress. The rest keep the clause active. Ellicott sees three tableaux, the Chaldaean power breaking treaties and removing landmarks, the summons to Elam and Media to end that tyranny, and the oppressed ceasing to sigh; he answers the argument that pairing Elam with Media proves a late date by noting that Sargon was at that time waging fierce war on both. Wesley says simply that the Medes and Persians used treachery as well as force.

John Calvin makes retaliation the point. Babylon had gained its power by plundering other nations and so seemed beyond danger, but having been a terror to others it could not avoid becoming a prey; that violence should answer violence is righteous, and when a stone is hard a hard hammer will be found to break it. Gill notes that the vision is called hard, harsh not to the prophet or the Jews but to the Chaldeans. Delitzsch, taking the next verse with this one, observes that what the prophet sees works on him like a horrible dream: he twists himself and does not hear, and the darkness of night that he loves is turned into quaking.
3:
Whose pangs these are divides the commentators. John Gill denies they can be the prophet's, since Babylon was his people's mortal enemy and the ceasing of their sighing could be no cause of distress to him but of joy; he puts the words in the mouth of the Babylonians, and of Belshazzar. John Calvin agrees: it was not enough simply to foretell the destruction, so the prophet assumes for the time the character of a Babylonian and sets the event before the eyes of the godly as in a mirror. Charles Ellicott takes the opposite view, that the vision is so terrible it overpowers all exultation and oppresses the prophet like a nightmare, and calls the suggestion of his identifying himself with the Babylonians and their night of revelry hardly tenable. Keil and Delitzsch read the agitation as the prophet's own. John Wesley keeps both, taking the night of pleasure for the prophet's own repose while allowing that it signified the horror to fall on Babylon in a night of feasting.

The banquet verse turns on the mood of its verbs. Adam Clarke observes that they stand in the infinitive absolute and should be rendered as statement, the table is prepared, on the analogy of a Latin idiom. Ellicott agrees they are better taken as indicative, they prepare and they watch, and reports rival renderings of the last clause as spreading the coverlet for the revellers' couches or taking a horoscope. Calvin allows they may be participles: while they were preparing the table and setting a guard, sudden terror arose. Gill and Wesley keep them as commands spoken by courtiers to remove the king's fears, with a watch set so the rest might indulge themselves more securely.

Both stop over the anointing of the shield. Wesley explains the custom, that shields were rubbed with oil to preserve and polish them and make them slippery, and takes the shield for all their weapons. Clarke reports that several rabbins understood the verse of Belshazzar's impious feast and death, and that since a king is his people's defence he is himself called the shield, so the order to anoint it means to anoint a new king, the old one having just been killed at table.

Calvin argues from the vividness itself: the ancient historian does not describe the storming of the city so historically as this, which shows it was not natural sagacity but heavenly inspiration that let the prophet describe unknown events. On the watchman he insists the same way, that the prophets neither learned from men nor foresaw by their own shrewdness, which is why they were called seers. Delitzsch supplies the unspoken link behind the connecting word, that they act so in Babylon because its destruction is determined, and observes that elsewhere the prophet stands on the watch-tower himself while here a distinct figure is posted.

The procession the watchman sees is described three ways. Clarke calls the passage extremely obscure from the ambiguity of the word used three times, which may mean a chariot, its rider, or a whole company, and suggests a cavalry in two parts or a force led by two riders, one on an ass and one on a camel, with the Medes and Persians distinguished by them. Delitzsch rules out both riding-animals and war-chariots and makes the word a troop seated upon animals, a long procession advancing quietly in serried ranks, like a caravan. Ellicott renders it a troop, a couple, and grounds the animals in history, both having served in the Persian army and both appearing by the thousand in the spoil an Assyrian king took from a Babylonian rebel. Gill names Cyrus and Darius outright; Wesley reads the whole as abundant warlike provision, chariots for carriage and for battle. Calvin explains the doubled report by distance: the first glance is confused, and only a nearer view makes the objects plain.
8:
The lion here is a person to some and a manner of speaking to others. John Gill has the watchman cry that he sees a lion, rejects the old identifications of the figure with named prophets, and makes it Cyrus at the head of the Median and Persian armies, likened to a lion for fierceness and strength, and a type of the Lion of Judah by whom mystical Babylon will fall. John Wesley agrees, and takes the lion for Cyrus or Darius leading their armies. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase as a lion and hears the low murmur of an eager, almost angry impatience. Keil and Delitzsch go furthest that way: the procession has vanished, the watchman sees and hears nothing, and he growls as if he were a lion, with the same dull angry sound and long breath out of full lungs, complaining that he has stood so long at his post for nothing.

Adam Clarke will have none of it, calling the received reading so unintelligible that he does not doubt the true word is the seer, differing by a letter, and that the Syriac translator found it so and rendered it watchman. John Calvin passes over the animal and uses the standing watch to confirm the prophecy: those whom God appoints to watch are neither drowsy nor dim-sighted, and their example stirs believers to the same attention.

Who announces the fall is a further question. Calvin denies the speaker can be the Babylonian king's watchman and weighs three candidates: God himself, whom he thinks likeliest, since the conqueror had no thought of overthrowing idols; the conqueror, who as God's servant is not unfitly made herald of the judgment; and the guardian of the vision, which suits the words best, as if an angel had added an interpretation. Ellicott makes the verse a second vision rather than the watchman's report of the first, the same cavalcade returning and no longer silent. Delitzsch sees at last where the procession went: it entered Babylon and mastered it, and a smaller troop now returns with the news. Both note that the cry is taken up in the last book of the Bible against a later Babylon; Ellicott adds that the stress falls on the smashing of the idols by iconoclastic Persians. Wesley assigns the explanation to the prophet and the act to God by Cyrus's hand.

The threshing of the closing verse is read of two peoples. Gill allows it might mean the Babylonians, threshed after being God's instrument on others, but prefers the Jews, whom the prophet calls his as his countrymen, and whom God calls his floor and his corn, afflicted for their own purging. Ellicott says the child of the threshing-floor is none other than Israel under invasion and exile, and adds that the prophet looks on those chastisements with yearning pity but cannot go beyond the word of the Lord, so what lies between the present distress and the distant deliverance stays hidden. Delitzsch reads it the same way and warns against being misled by a later prophet who turned the same figure differently. Wesley alone thinks it spoken of Babylon, and explains the idiom that the threshing stands for the corn threshed and the corn for a people sorely afflicted.

Clarke keeps to image and grammar, glossing the address as spoken to whatever lies under the afflicting hand like corn spread on the floor to be threshed and winnowed, and noting that the translators used the word in a passive sense for the thing threshed. Calvin ends where he began: the splendour of the monarchy made the prediction of its ruin seem fabulous, so the prophet leads their minds to God. The two phrases mean one thing, in the Hebrew manner of saying a thing twice, and the passage should correct the natural vice of measuring God's power by our own standard.
11:
Everyone agrees this oracle is dark, and most that it is not about the place it names. John Gill reports that some rabbis take Dumah for the son of Ishmael and his Arabian descendants, but holds for Edom, since Seir is named here and a separate word on Arabia follows; the Greek renders the title the vision of Idumea, and one rabbinic copy was found reading Edom outright. Adam Clarke reports the same variant. Keil and Delitzsch reason from geography: a question called from the mountains south of Palestine cannot be answered by any of the three known places of the name, in eastern Hauran, on the northern caravan road, or in the hills of Judah. Charles Ellicott concludes the name is mystical, Edom altered to a word meaning silence, and that as in the opening oracle the silence is first of expectancy and then of desolation. John Calvin alone keeps the descent from Ishmael and calls them Dumeans.

Matthew Henry does not decide, but draws the use. Some of Israel's neighbours are meant, and their distress foretold not only to prepare them but to warn Israel not to lean on any nation round about; we must see creature confidences failing us, and feel them breaking under us, that we may not lay more weight on them than they will bear. The explication is difficult, he grants, because no history records the accomplishment, but the application is easy; and the one calling out of Seir was more concerned for the public safety than his countrymen, who were careless and secure. John Wesley takes the whole as a dialogue, the people of Dumah speaking by one of their number to a watchman set as men do in great danger, coming early to learn what the night had brought; the doubled question, he says, shows their solicitude.

The answer divides them further. Gill hears a standing succession of morning and night: the gospel morning dispersing the shadows of the law, a night of blindness on the Jews, a morning at the Reformation, and a night now begun in coldness and error. Ellicott keeps to Edom and reads the rhythm historically, a morning of hope whose day closes too quickly in blackness, summing up a future of one conqueror after another, a brief rising, and the present desolation. Wesley makes it immediate: the night is past without mischief and the light approaching, but the morning will be gone and the night return, and their fears with it. Calvin makes it duration rather than sequence, the watchman saying in effect that what he tells them today he will tell them tomorrow: that wretched condition of hanging in doubt between death and life which was threatened as a curse through Moses. Delitzsch, noting that the reply is deliberately cast in an Aramaic form of Hebrew, thinks Luther hit the sense, that when the morning comes it will still be night, though the connective cannot be stretched to mean and yet.

The closing summons is read as dismissal or invitation. Ellicott takes the prophet to decline answering: if they like to ask they may, and return from a bootless journey; the reading of that word as a call to repentance he rejects, since we should then have expected a turning to the Lord. Calvin offers two senses, that they will lose their pains by running to and fro, or that the more anxious may go to Dumah and tremble worse there than at home; nowhere will they be safe, and the Church, he adds, has no safer retreat than God. Wesley reads an appointment to come again next morning, and so from morning to morning. Clarke, having given the sense that the Jews would be delivered from captivity and the Edomites not, breaks off honestly: what the last line means he cannot pretend to divine, and the Hebrew manuscripts give no assistance.
13:
The heading of this last oracle is suspected by three readers. Adam Clarke calls the title of doubtful authority: it is missing from many Greek copies, the word for burden is elsewhere joined to its object without a preposition, and the same phrase stands as the second word of the prophecy itself, so a marginal note might easily have slipped into the text. Keil and Delitzsch put the difficulty the other way: the other three headings take a simple genitive, and this one alone would be unsymbolic, so the added letter must have been introduced to make it symbolic, the prophet pointing it one way while holding the other in mind. Charles Ellicott takes the alteration for a deliberate play, Arabia turned into a word for evening, the land spoken of being a land of shadow with evening falling on it.

Matthew Henry supplies the descent and the use. The Dedanites came from Abraham by Keturah, the men of Tema and Kedar from Ishmael; the Arabians lived in tents and kept cattle, and the Jews probably depended on them as a wall against the more warlike eastern nations, so hearing this burden was meant to alarm them. John Wesley reads the lodging in the forest as implying that a populous country would become wilderness, notes that travellers there went and still go in companies, and makes the Dedanites merchants trading with Tyre. Ellicott adds that Assyrian armies would force them off their trade routes into the desert. John Calvin observes that the prophet leaves unnoticed none of the nations known to the Jews.

The bread and water brought to the fugitives is the crux. Ellicott has the Dedanites driven off their route with provisions failing, and the men of Tema, afraid to invite them in lest the invader strike them too, carrying out food secretly, their hospitality practised in strange contrast with Arab custom. Calvin reads the clause as exhortation, the Arabians arriving destitute and needing to be met, and reports that some take the words as mockery of a people who had been cruel to the Jews. Clarke changes the geography rather than the tone, reading with the Greek and Latin the southern country instead of Tema, since its men were probably caught in the same calamity and in no condition to help; bringing out bread and water, he adds, is ordinary humanity, the more so in deserts where water is hard to come by. John Gill keeps the Temanites as Arabians assisting their countrymen.

On the flight Ellicott notices that the fourfold repetition of the fuller preposition marks the stages of the retreat, and Calvin that the enemy pursues with arms so that flight is the only safety, the whole foretold so the Jews might learn that providence governs the world.

The term set to it is read as a guarantee. Ellicott says the formula of the hireling's years expresses the most precise measurement and so offers a test of the forecast, Kedar standing generically for the nomad tribes. Calvin finds comfort in the nearness, since we are naturally fiery and do not willingly bear delay, and God takes our weakness into account when he says he hastens his work. Wesley makes it an exact year from the prophecy, executed by the Assyrians. On the archers, Gill notes that the Kedarenes were expert with the bow for wild beasts and men alike, following their ancestor Ishmael. Calvin reads the double stroke as pursuit of the ungodly to the utmost, where the punishment of the godly is moderated so they are not destroyed. Ellicott hears in the word for residue the prophet's characteristic remnant and refers it to the Assyrian kings who record their victories over the Arabian tribes. Clarke transposes two words with the Latin to read the mighty bowmen, and compares the closing formula with the Roman verses on Cannae ending, Jupiter has thus spoken.
